title: Supercommunicators
author: Charles Duhigg
blurb: Why do some people connect with almost anyone, while others keep missing each other even when they agree? Charles Duhigg argues the difference is a learnable skill, not a gift. Drawing on research and stories from places like the CIA, hospitals and TV writers' rooms, he shows that most discussions are really three kinds of conversation at once. One is practical, about what this is really about. One is emotional, about how we feel. One is social, about who we are. Supercommunicators notice which one is happening and match it. They ask deep questions, prove they are listening, and make room for people's identities. They also set ground rules when conversations get hard. The result is what Duhigg calls a learning conversation, where both people understand each other better. Anyone can practise it, whether at work, at home or online.

lessons.b: Most conversations mix three kinds at once, practical, emotional and social, and miscommunication happens when people are having different kinds without realising it.
Connection happens when we notice which kind of conversation the other person is having and meet them there, instead of pulling them into ours.
In practical conversations, openly sharing your goals and asking what the other person wants turns a tug of war into joint problem solving.
Asking about values, beliefs and experiences, rather than just facts, invites people to share feelings and builds real closeness quickly.
In conflict, repeating back what you heard in your own words and checking you got it right shows people they are understood, which lowers defences.

lessons.t: Who Are We? Identity Shapes Hearing
lessons.b: Our social identities shape how we hear a message, so good communicators acknowledge the many identities people hold and look for ones they share.

(fix: Redraw the handshake as a clean, simple icon. Place it fully inside the overlap region, for example centred below the 'SAME WORRY' text and above the lower intersection, with clear space from both circle outlines. Or replace it with a simple amber dot or star marker.)

scene 4: The struck-through 'OBSTACLE' label sits almost directly against the bottom of the parent's chair legs, so the chair and the text nearly touch and crowd together. (fix: Move the 'OBSTACLE' label and the 'Thoughtful protector' label down by about 20–30px, or shorten the chair legs, so there is a clear gap between the chair and the text.)

lessons.b: Notice the kind of conversation, share goals, ask about and share feelings, and explore identities, and every conversation becomes a chance to truly understand each other.
